newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Yugoslavia seen needing outside help for banks.
newsitem.headline: Yugoslavia seen needing outside help for banks.

text.p: Yugoslavia cannot help ailing domestic banks without assistance but foreign funds will come in only after it rejoins world financial bodies and reschedules debt, economists said on Thursday.
"There will be no bank rehabilitation without fresh foreign funds," Miroljub Labus, chief economist at the Economics Institute, said.
"Whatever we do about banks can only be some kind of preparation for a real bank rehabilitation. But I do not believe that centralisation of the banking system is a good way to prepare," he added.

Yugoslavia must first rejoin the International Monetary Fund (IMF), World Bank and other financial institutions and then negotiate a debt rescheduling agreement with its commercial creditors, Labus said.
Yugoslavia has been banned from access to the IMF, World Bank and world capital markets since U.N. sanctions were imposed in 1992.
Sanctions were lifted formally in October 1996 but Yugoslavia remained under the so-called outer wall of sanctions keeping it away from the world capital markets.

To regain access to foreign funds, Belgrade has to cooperate with the Hague War Crimes Tribunal, improve human rights in its majority-Albanian southern province of Kosovo and speed up negotiations with other republics of the former Balkan federation on division of assets.

"Once we rejoin the IMF and win a debt rescheduling agreement, money will start flowing in. Only then can we begin with real bank rehabilitation. But there will be no money until then and no bank rehabilitation," Labus said.

Economists cast doubt on some state banks' plans to clean up big state banking groups balances of external debt by setting up special in-bank agencies to take over foreign debts and claims of local banks and companies.
Apart from those liabilities, the bank overhaul programme is planned to clear bank balances from frozen savings.
Yugoslavia's foreign debt is unofficially estimated at around $9 billion. The state owes a further $4 billion to its citizens for private savings frozen in 1991.
Economists said a pure book-keeping clean-up of bank balances would not provide banks with the additional funds needed to kick-start capital-starved industries.
They also feared the move will lead to further centralisation of the financial sector and provide the government with even more control over scarce finances.
Labus said international financial institutions will not support the creation of any cartels in the banking sector.

"In practice, monopolies in this economy have widened to the financial sector. Any competition is squeezed out, and that is no way towards bank overhaul. And world financial bodies will certainly not give support to any such programme.
"Monopolies are no good because they compete and challenge legal institutions," Labus added.

Economists said the only way to make Yugoslav banks more efficient was to introduce more competition in the sector, which numbers 100 banks. Of these 40 are state-owned, mostly concentrated in five big banking groups.
The rest are private and commercial banks.
Nebojsa Savic, vice-president of the private BK University, said the state had to allow the creation of new banks.
"It is one thing to rehabilitate big state banks. But, with new private banks, there will be more competition within the sector," Savic told Reuters.
Savic said he suspected Yugoslavia was trying to follow Slovenia, which several years ago set up a new Ljubljanska Banka to take over external debts and claims from other banks.
